title: Trump administration dismisses crisis fears after string of disruptive tech outages | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Top officials from the Trump administration sought to reassure Americans and dismiss fears of a possible crisis after a string of major tech and infrastructure failures disrupted travel, business, and banking for millions of people.

“We do not see some crisis coming down.But you have to be prepared for everything,” US Vice President JD Vance told Fox News inan interview released Monday.

Vance said that friends had asked him whether they should be building bunkers or stocking up on food and water. “My answer to that is no,” he said, adding that reports of Pentagon bases preparing to operate off the grid for 90 days – and similar reports of European countries urging citizens to stock up on supplies – are just “basic good government.”

“Making sure that our military would be prepared, God forbid if there was a crisis,” Vance said, “but we don’t see a crisis coming down the pike.”

Vance’s comments come after a chaotic week of tech disruption and confusion. Even former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt urged the Trump administration to be transparent with Americans about the issues.

“I’m wondering the same thing: what’s happening? I’m checking my bank account with a little bit of worry, and what I would say to the White House is transparency is key. It’s going to help the country grapple with what’s going on,” she said.

Last Thursday,a massive Microsoft outageleft people worldwide without access to Outlook email, Teams meeting tools and other staples of modern office life. Microsoft said it was caused by a “technical issue,” which took roughly two days to fix – costing potentially$7 billionin lost productivity by some estimates.

That outage hadn’t even been fully resolved before theFederal Aviation Administrationexperienceda systems failureon Friday – causing thousands of flights to be canceled, throwing airports into chaos, and stranding millions of travelers just before the weekend. The FAA suspectsthe crisis was caused bysingle newly-installed routerin a remote radio outpost in Arkansas.

Then, on Monday, major banks reported issues. Thousands ofChase Bankcustomers had trouble using their online accounts, as well as making transactions at physical branches, which the company said was related to a “software bug.” Customers reported issues at other major banks, including Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and U.S. Bank, though on a smaller scale – which appearedto be related to sending money through Zelle, a digital payment network, to Chase accounts.

Later Monday afternoon, United Airlines reported a widespread but short-lived system outage thatdelayed some outbound flights. It lasted about 30 minutes, with fewer than 150 flights impacted, a United Airlines spokesperson told CNN. And on Tuesday, CNN reported that the highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal written communicationswas down, according to six people familiar with the matter.

Speaking before that report, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said in media interviews there was no evidence to suggest the reports of technological issues were directly related. Nor, he said, were they the product of hacking.

“I can tell you with 98% certainty, we’re not seeing the cyber attack, no one is out there taking claim for it, we’re not seeing the traffic, we’re not seeing the footprints going in, we’re not seeing the footprints going out — and so nothing points to it being connected,” he said on Fox News Monday.

Mullin was even more unequivocal in an interview with CNBC Tuesday, saying, “I can tell you with complete certainty that we are not under attack. There’s no cyber threat that’s taken place. The homeland is very secure.”

“If we had somebody to blame, it’d be great, because we’d be able to punch them back,” he added.

Mullin said the problems appeared to stem from the fact that companies were “pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system a little bit, and it’s not able to catch up.”

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton echoed his remarks in a Fox interview Tuesday, saying there was no indication of a “coordinated cyber attack” or “state-sponsored activity.”

“Everybody recognizes it’s time to upgrade their systems, and as they upgrade them, they’re not coming back as expected in all cases,” he said. “But this is just an upgrade in patching, an upgrade in systems and, like I said, looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyber-attack incident.”

Some experts agree, and warn that this technological overload actually is the thread tying together the past week’s meltdowns.

“I think it’s connected in the sense that a lot of our infrastructure in this country, in the world, is aging,” said Alex Hamerstone, cybersecurity expert at security consulting firm TrustedSec.

“It’s constantly evolving and changing, and our dependence on these technical systems is growing every day … Everything is becoming more technically connected and more complex.”

Vance acknowledged this in his Fox News interview, saying the administration had invested in rebuilding and replacing old infrastructure – but that a larger overhaul would require more resources approved by Congress.

“The problem is we are dealing with 50-year-old technology. It works most of the time,” he said. “Sometimes you have to work on a patchwork of solutions to keep a 50-year-old system up and running. Why do we have a 50-year-old system in the first place?”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy issued a demand this weekend for as much as $50 billion in emergency funding after the FAA ground stop – but key Republicans, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune, are demanding more information about that request, including what the administration had done with previous funding.

Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to update air traffic control systems – which many lawmakers, including Thune, have argued has not yet been fully spent.

This story has been updated with additional developments.

CNN’s Piper Hudspeth Blackburn and Kit Maher contributed to this report.

CNN’s Piper Hudspeth Blackburn and Kit Maher contributed to this report.
